data.reasoning: Both models reviewed the same 5 files (PKGBUILD, .SRCINFO, .gitignore, .nvchecker.toml, LICENSE). The PKGBUILD contains a standard Rust build process with a pinned GitHub release tarball (v17.10.1) and valid SHA256 checksum. All build functions use typical cargo commands with --frozen/--locked flags. The only disagreement stems from a tool error in the qwen report: the LICENSE file audit failed with HTTP 400 BadRequestError, causing an inconclusive verdict. The deepseek model successfully audited LICENSE and correctly identified it as a standard ISC-style license text with no executable code. No injection patterns, no suspicious network requests, no obfuscated code, and no execution of fetched content were found in any file.
data.disagreement_analysis: The disagreement is caused by a tool error, not genuine security uncertainty. The qwen model's API request failed when auditing the LICENSE file (HTTP 400 BadRequestError), resulting in an inconclusive file verdict that propagated to the overall package verdict. The deepseek model successfully audited the same LICENSE file and found it to be standard license text. This is a false disagreement caused by infrastructure failure, not conflicting security analysis.
coverage_issues: qwen model: LICENSE file audit failed due to HTTP 400 BadRequestError, causing inconclusive verdict
learnings: Tool errors (API failures, timeouts) should not propagate to package-level inconclusive verdicts when the failed file is low-risk (e.g., LICENSE, README, .gitignore). The audit tool should distinguish between 'failed to audit due to infrastructure error' and 'found suspicious content'.

Standard text files without executable code (LICENSE, README, .gitignore) should be auto-classified as safe when audit fails due to transient errors, since they cannot contain injection payloads that execute during makepkg.
When multiple models agree on a verdict but one has tool errors, the consensus from successful audits should take precedence over the error-induced inconclusive.
